name: Populism
info: Populism is a contested concept for political stances that set the common people against a perceived elite; the term developed in the late 19th century and has been applied to movements, parties and leaders on the left and the right across every continent.

facts.thinkers: Hélio Jaguaribe, whose 1954 text is considered the first academic study of Latin American populism; Edward Shils, who proposed populism in 1954 as a term for anti-elite trends in US society; Richard Hofstadter and Daniel Bell, who read the People's Party as status anxiety; Gino Germani and Seymour Martin Lipset, on mass mobilisation; Ernesto Laclau of the Essex School, who treats populism as a discursive logic; Cas Mudde and Cristóbal Rovira Kaltwasser, who call it a thin-centred ideology; Kurt Weyland, who defines it as a political strategy
facts.texts: Léon Lemonnier's 1929 manifesto of the populist novel; the National People's Party's first national platform of 1892; Hélio Jaguaribe's 1954 study of Latin American populism; Edward Shils's 1954 article on anti-elite trends in the United States
facts.ideas: a society divided between the pure people and a corrupt elite; the general will of the people; the common sense of the people set above expert and institutional knowledge; distrust of representative institutions and a preference for direct decisions such as referendums; a charismatic leader as the voice of the people; a style of politics that breaks with the manners of the established elite
facts.today: The term is applied to parties and leaders on both left and right, among them Greece's Syriza, Spain's Podemos, India's Aam Aadmi Party, Austria's Freedom Party, the Swiss People's Party and Argentina's Justicialist Party, and scholars still disagree over whether it is a useful category at all

t: Populism has no single agreed definition: scholars treat it as a thin-centred ideology, a class phenomenon, a discursive logic, a political style, a strategy for winning power or a pattern of economic policy, and some have proposed abandoning the word.

The word first appeared in English in 1858 and took hold through the United States People's Party of the 1880s to early 1900s, while the Russian narodniki of the 1860s and 1870s, often translated as populists, differed from it in ideology and course.

Scholars sharply disagree on its relation to democracy: some define it as inherently anti-democratic, others as a democratic impulse that empowers marginalised groups, and others hold that it takes contradictory forms depending on context.
dyk: Between 1950 and 1960 roughly 160 publications on populism were recorded, and by 2018 the number of academic papers and books with the term in their title or abstract had grown to 615 in a single year; the Cambridge Dictionary chose "populism" as its Word of the Year in 2017.
ev: The word "populist" first appears in English, as an antonym for "aristocratic" in a translation of a work by Alphonse de Lamartine
The National People's Party adopts its first national platform in the United States, which calls for protecting the rights of urban workmen

The mass mobilisation of 17 October in Argentina, often considered the founding moment of Peronism
Edward Shils in the United States and Hélio Jaguaribe in Brazil publish the texts that turn populism into an academic concept
A conference at the London School of Economics fails to produce a unified theory of populism
The election of Donald Trump and the United Kingdom's vote to leave the European Union are widely read as expressions of populist sentiment

sections.origins:
The word "populist" first appeared in English in 1858, as an antonym for "aristocratic" in a translation of a work by Alphonse de Lamartine. In the Russian Empire of the 1860s and 1870s the term was associated with the narodniki, a left-leaning agrarian movement whose name is often translated as "populists". It aimed to transfer political power to the peasant communes through a radical programme of agrarian reform, and some historians have described it as an intellectual and organisational precursor of later revolutionary movements in Russia. In English the term gained broader prominence through the United States People's Party and its predecessors, active between the 1880s and the early 1900s. The party championed small-scale farmers, advocated expansionist monetary policies and accessible credit, and was relatively progressive for its time on questions of women's and minority rights.

Although both the Russian and the American movements have been labelled populist, they differed in ideological content and historical trajectory. In early 20th-century France the term moved into literature, naming a genre of novel that portrayed the lives of the lower classes sympathetically: Léon Lemonnier published a manifesto for it in 1929 and Antonine Coullet-Tessier established a prize for it in 1931. Some scholars have also retrospectively associated populism with the democracy of classical Athens, the Levellers of seventeenth-century England and the Protestant Reformation.
sections.ideas:
Because the term is used for a broad and often contradictory array of movements, there is no single doctrine to describe, and the main theoretical approaches define it differently. The ideational approach of Cas Mudde and Cristóbal Rovira Kaltwasser defines populism as a "thin-centred ideology" that divides society into two antagonistic groups, "the pure people" and "the corrupt elite", and sees politics as an expression of the general will of the people. It attaches itself to broader movements such as socialism or conservatism, and so appears on both the left and the right. In this view the people's common sense is held to be superior to elite expertise, and representative democracy is criticised in favour of direct decisions such as referendums.

Other approaches put the weight elsewhere. Ernesto Laclau treated populism as a discursive logic in which unmet demands coalesce around a symbol that names a popular movement against an elite. The performative approach of Pierre Ostiguy, Benjamin Moffitt and María Esperanza Casullo sees a political style: rhetoric, gestures and staging that break with the norms of respectable politics. Kurt Weyland defined it as a strategy of a personalist leader who governs through direct, unmediated and uninstitutionalised support from large numbers of mostly unorganised followers. Economists such as Rudiger Dornbusch, Jeffrey Sachs and Sebastián Edwards used the word for expansive public spending financed by foreign loans and followed by inflationary crises and austerity.
sections.spread:
In North America populism was often characterised by regional mobilisation and loose organisation. In the late 19th and early 20th centuries it was widespread in the western provinces of Canada and in the southwest and Great Plains of the United States, where it combined with agrarianism as "prairie populism" and set small independent farmers against the bankers and politicians of the northeast. Later American examples included the Greenback Party, Robert M. La Follette's Progressive Party of 1924 and Huey P. Long's Share Our Wealth movement of 1933 to 1935, and in Canada the social credit groups of the 1930s to the 1960s. After the Second World War right-wing populist parties emerged in Europe, among them Guglielmo Giannini's Common Man's Front in Italy and Pierre Poujade's union in France.

In Latin America the term entered political language after the war. A first wave, lasting until the 1960s, brought leaders such as Getúlio Vargas in Brazil and Juan Domingo Perón in Argentina; a second, in the late 1980s and early 1990s, Carlos Menem, Fernando Collor de Mello and Alberto Fujimori; a third, from the late 1990s, the left-wing governments of the pink tide. In Africa, populism became apparent in the 1980s according to Danielle Resnick, with military leaders such as Jerry Rawlings in Ghana and Thomas Sankara in Burkina Faso. In South East Asia populist politicians emerged after the 1997 Asian financial crisis, and in India the term has been applied to caste mobilisation and later to the Bharatiya Janata Party.
sections.power:
The record of populists in power differs by case and by definition. Ideational scholars note that not all populists are authoritarian and that populism in opposition can mobilise groups who feel excluded and draw attention to popular grievances, but they generally contend that it becomes detrimental to pluralism once in power. By claiming to represent the authentic will of the people, they argue, populists, particularly on the right, may concentrate executive power and bypass or undermine institutions such as the judiciary and the media, a dynamic that can give rise to what John Stuart Mill called the "tyranny of the majority".

In Latin America, Vargas and Perón organised labour unions and drew previously excluded groups into national politics. Marxist critics such as Francisco Weffort, Fernando Henrique Cardoso and Octavio Ianni acknowledged this integration but argued that it stayed within a bourgeois framework and that populist regimes subordinated trade unions to state control; other historians argue that the period saw growing politicisation of workers. Menem, Collor and Fujimori combined anti-elite rhetoric with neoliberal reforms, often in line with recommendations of the International Monetary Fund, while Hugo Chávez promoted participatory structures such as Communal Councils. In Africa, Rawlings and Sankara came to power in coups, claiming to represent the voice of the people and setting up participatory organisations. In South East Asia the populist administrations of Joseph Estrada, Roh Moo-hyun, Chen Shui-bian and Thaksin Shinawatra were removed soon after taking power. In the United States the People's Party won seats in several state legislatures in the 1890s but never mounted a successful presidential challenge.
sections.critiques:
Criticism of populism and criticism of the concept run together. In the 1950s and 1960s Richard Hofstadter and Daniel Bell reinterpreted the People's Party through a critical lens as an expression of status anxiety and irrationalism, and compared the anti-elitism of the 1890s Populists with that of Joseph McCarthy; not all academics accepted the comparison. Liberal scholars such as Steven Levitsky and Daniel Ziblatt argue that authoritarian-leaning populists become viable only when traditional elites accommodate them, and that backsliding follows when elites abandon informal norms of mutual toleration. Karl Loewenstein's idea of militant democracy holds that democracies may sometimes take exceptional restrictive measures to defend themselves. Mudde and Rovira Kaltwasser, though critical of populism, caution against dismissing populists as irrational, since this reinforces the binary of pure people and corrupt elite.

Each definition has its own critics. The ideational approach is said to proceed deductively and to impose assumptions of moral dualism; the strategic approach, by focusing on leaders, excludes parties and movements such as the People's Party; the economic definition, critics argue, reduces populism to left-wing mismanagement and stigmatises heterodox policies. Scholars influenced by Laclau hold that populism is inherently emancipatory and pluralistic, and that authoritarian nationalist movements often called populist are better described as fascist. Some scholars have proposed abandoning the word, since its conflation with far-right nativism misrepresents self-described historical populists, while others hold the concept too integral to political analysis to discard.
sections.legacy:
Until the 1950s academics used the word mostly for historians of the People's Party. Edward Shils's article of 1954 on McCarthyism and Hélio Jaguaribe's text of the same year on Brazil opened its wider use, and a conference at the London School of Economics in 1967 failed to produce a shared theory. About 160 publications on populism were recorded between 1950 and 1960 and over 1,500 between 1990 and 2000. After the political events of 2016 the term gained unprecedented global prominence, and the annual count of papers with it in the title or abstract rose from 95 on average in 2000 to 2015 to 615 in 2018. Its use has taken a more negative tone, and it has often been conflated with demagoguery.

Scholars have proposed many causes, among them economic grievance, the losses of modernisation, a cultural backlash against postmaterialist values, post-democracy and the media, with mixed empirical support. The protests that followed the 2008 financial crisis, including Occupy, the Indignados and the Gilets jaunes, have been described as populist, as have parties that grew out of them, such as Podemos and India's Aam Aadmi Party. Some European states have adopted a cordon sanitaire, in which mainstream parties refuse to form coalitions with populist or extremist actors. On the left, Chantal Mouffe argues for a left populist project that mobilises passion for democratic and egalitarian ends.

summary: Populism is a contested concept for politics that set the common people against a perceived elite. The word dates from 1858 and spread through the United States People's Party of the 1880s to early 1900s; scholars define it as an ideology, a style, a strategy or an economic pattern, and disagree on how it relates to democracy.
references: Benjamin Moffitt, The Global Rise of Populism: Performance, Political Style, and Representation (Stanford University Press, 2016)
Cas Mudde, Populism: A Very Short Introduction (Oxford University Press, 2017)
notes: Start 1880, circa true: the article gives the People's Party and its predecessors as active 'between the 1880s and early 1900s' and says the term 'developed in the late 19th century'; the word appears in English in 1858 and the narodniki are of the 1860s-1870s. Region is Americas as given; the article calls the Russian narodniki 'widely regarded as the first populist movement', which I left out of the text since it names a first elsewhere.
The article has no key founding text of populism; 'texts' lists only the works and documents it names with a year. The 1892 platform date is the article's (a parenthesis, not closed in the source).
Lipset's distinction (fascism from the middle classes, populism from the poor) left out of the sections.

Left out: the Boulangists, the völkisch movement, the national sections on Israel, the Middle East, Oceania, Brazil's recent presidents, Milei and Trump's and Sanders's campaigns (present politics), and the detailed party-system studies.
Article text 'tyranny of the majority' is attributed to Mill by the article. 'Sub-Saharan Africa' section says populism 'rare'; I used only the 1980s military leaders as the article's first case.
The article lists 'The People's Party ... 1892' platform inside brackets in the North America section; I wrote 'National People's Party' as the article does there.
